turns.text:
My wife is treating me like a criminal over money from my own account. In March my little brother left a shared house where he didn't feel safe anymore, and he needed a deposit to get into a new place fast. I lent him six thousand dollars from my personal savings. Not our house fund. He's already started paying it back.

Yes, I should have told her sooner, and I've said so. I was going to tell her once he'd paid some of it back, so it wouldn't turn into a whole thing. Then he mentioned it at dinner before I got the chance.

In February she bought a $3,500 bike and told me the next day. I didn't make it a referendum on our marriage. Now she's spent two nights at her sister's, and every talk ends with "I don't know if I can trust you with money." I think she's never really accepted my family, and this gives her a reason. He's my brother. What was I supposed to do, leave him somewhere he didn't feel safe?

What do you make of this?

Helping your brother get out of a place where he didn't feel safe was a good thing to do. You don't need to apologize for that, and I don't think it's really what she's upset about.

I think the hard part is this. The loan was in March, and she found out at dinner, from him, months later. Your plan was to tell her once some had been repaid "so it wouldn't turn into a whole thing." That means you knew it would matter to her and decided to manage when and how she found out. From her side, it isn't "he lent his brother money." It's "he made a significant financial decision, kept it from me on purpose, and I found out in front of his family." Learning it that way can feel humiliating, like everyone at the table knew something about her own marriage that she didn't.

That's also why the bike comparison may not land the way you want it to. Spending without asking first is the same in both cases, but she told you the next day. You waited months and would have kept waiting if he hadn't brought it up. Arguably neither of you should spend that kind of money without a conversation first, and that's worth raising. But one was a disclosure delay of a day, and the other was a decision not to disclose. If you lead with the bike, she'll probably hear deflection, and it'll pull the conversation away from what she needs to hear.

The same goes for "she's never accepted my family." Maybe there's real tension there, and maybe it deserves its own conversation. But if you bring it up now, it turns her hurt about being kept in the dark into a story about her bias. Notice that she isn't saying "you shouldn't help your brother." She's saying "I don't know if I can trust you with money." That's about you and her, not about him.

You've said you should have told her sooner. Saying it is a start, but what usually rebuilds trust is showing you understand why it hurt, without a "but" attached. Something like: "I hid it because I didn't want to deal with your reaction, and that wasn't fair to you. You found out in a way that made you feel like an outsider in your own marriage. I'm sorry." Then propose something concrete, like a threshold above which you both talk before spending or lending, from any account, including her bike-type purchases going forward. That gives you a fair way to address the February thing as a shared rule rather than a counterattack.

Two nights at her sister's sounds like she's hurt and needs space, not necessarily that she's done. If the conversations keep going in circles, a couple of sessions with a counselor can help, mostly because money secrecy tends to be about something deeper for both people.

Is there anything about how those talks have gone that makes you feel she doesn't want to resolve this?

Partly, and the parts matter differently.

You're right that helping your brother was a good, decent thing to do. You're also right that big spending without a conversation has happened on both sides, and that's fair to address as a shared problem.

But on what's actually breaking things right now, no, I don't think you are. You kept it from her for months on purpose, and she found out at a family dinner. Her reaction to that isn't her treating you like a criminal or rejecting your family. It's a pretty understandable response to finding out she was managed instead of told.

I know that's not what you were hoping to hear. If you go back to her looking to be right, I think you'll get more nights at her sister's. If you go back wanting to understand why this hurt her and offering a real fix, you have a good chance of getting through it. You clearly care about the people close to you. That's what you did for your brother, and she needs to see you do it for her too.
